questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Lung volumes, compliance, V/Q & mechanics of breathing
questions.stem: Which lung volume cannot be measured by simple spirometry?
questions.concept: Residual volume, and therefore functional residual capacity and total lung capacity, require helium dilution, nitrogen washout or body plethysmography since this air cannot be exhaled.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Lung volumes, compliance, V/Q & mechanics of breathing
questions.stem: Functional residual capacity is the sum of:
options: Expiratory reserve volume and residual volume
questions.concept: FRC is the resting volume where inward elastic recoil of the lung balances outward recoil of the chest wall. It falls in pregnancy, obesity and supine posture, and rises in emphysema.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Lung volumes, compliance, V/Q & mechanics of breathing
questions.stem: Surfactant reduces surface tension and thereby:
options: Increases compliance and prevents alveolar collapse, particularly of small alveoli
questions.concept: By the Laplace relation, pressure is proportional to tension divided by radius, so without surfactant small alveoli would empty into larger ones. Surfactant lowers tension more in small alveoli, stabilising them.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Lung volumes, compliance, V/Q & mechanics of breathing
questions.stem: Physiological dead space differs from anatomical dead space by including:
options: Alveoli that are ventilated but not perfused
questions.concept: In health the two are nearly equal. Physiological dead space rises markedly in pulmonary embolism, where perfusion is lost to ventilated alveoli - the physiological basis of the raised alveolar-arterial gradient.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Lung volumes, compliance, V/Q & mechanics of breathing
questions.stem: A ventilation-perfusion ratio of zero represents:
options: A true shunt, where perfused alveoli receive no ventilation
questions.concept: Shunt causes hypoxaemia that does not correct with 100% oxygen, distinguishing it from V/Q mismatch. Consolidation, atelectasis and pulmonary oedema are common causes.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Lung volumes, compliance, V/Q & mechanics of breathing
questions.stem: In the upright lung, ventilation and perfusion are both greatest at:
options: The base, with perfusion increasing more than ventilation so V/Q is lowest there
questions.concept: Gravity produces higher V/Q at the apex, favouring tuberculosis reactivation, and lower V/Q at the base. The West zones describe the relationship of alveolar, arterial and venous pressures.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Lung volumes, compliance, V/Q & mechanics of breathing
questions.stem: The main muscle of quiet inspiration is:
options: The diaphragm, accounting for about 75 percent of tidal volume
questions.concept: Quiet expiration is passive, driven by elastic recoil. Accessory muscles - sternocleidomastoid, scalenes and abdominals - are recruited in exercise and respiratory distress, and their use is a clinical sign of severity.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Lung volumes, compliance, V/Q & mechanics of breathing
questions.stem: Compliance of the lung is reduced in:
questions.concept: Restrictive disease stiffens the lung requiring greater pressure for a given volume change. Emphysema destroys elastic tissue increasing compliance but reducing recoil, causing air trapping.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Lung volumes, compliance, V/Q & mechanics of breathing
questions.stem: The Hering-Breuer inflation reflex:
options: Limits excessive lung inflation via vagal stretch receptors, important in newborns
Operates during quiet breathing in adults
Is mediated by the phrenic nerve
questions.concept: It is largely inactive during quiet adult breathing, becoming important at tidal volumes above about 1 litre and in the newborn, protecting against overdistension.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Lung volumes, compliance, V/Q & mechanics of breathing
questions.stem: In obstructive lung disease, spirometry characteristically shows:
questions.concept: Restrictive disease shows a preserved or raised ratio with reduced FVC and total lung capacity. Bronchodilator reversibility of more than 12% and 200 mL supports asthma over COPD.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Respiratory regulation, high altitude & diving
questions.stem: The most important stimulus to respiration under normal conditions is:
options: Arterial carbon dioxide tension acting on central chemoreceptors
questions.concept: Central chemoreceptors in the medulla respond to hydrogen ions generated from carbon dioxide crossing the blood-brain barrier. Hypoxic drive via peripheral chemoreceptors becomes significant only below about 60 mmHg.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Respiratory regulation, high altitude & diving
questions.stem: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid body respond primarily to:
options: A fall in arterial oxygen tension
questions.concept: They also respond to raised carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions, and become the dominant drive in chronic carbon dioxide retention - the basis of caution with high-flow oxygen in some COPD patients.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Respiratory regulation, high altitude & diving
questions.stem: At high altitude, the initial physiological response is:
questions.concept: Hypoxic ventilatory drive produces alkalosis which itself limits ventilation, until renal bicarbonate excretion over days restores pH and permits full acclimatisation - the rationale for graded ascent.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Respiratory regulation, high altitude & diving
questions.stem: Acetazolamide prevents acute mountain sickness by:
options: Causing bicarbonate diuresis and metabolic acidosis which stimulates ventilation
questions.concept: It accelerates the renal compensation that would otherwise take days. Definitive treatment of severe altitude illness including cerebral or pulmonary oedema is immediate descent.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Respiratory regulation, high altitude & diving
questions.stem: Chronic acclimatisation to high altitude involves:
options: Increased 2,3-DPG, polycythaemia and raised capillary density
questions.concept: Raised 2,3-DPG shifts the oxygen dissociation curve rightward aiding tissue unloading. Excessive polycythaemia causes chronic mountain sickness (Monge disease) with hyperviscosity.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Respiratory regulation, high altitude & diving
questions.stem: Decompression sickness in divers results from:
options: Nitrogen bubbles forming as dissolved gas comes out of solution on rapid ascent
questions.concept: Bubbles cause joint pain (bends), respiratory distress (chokes) and neurological deficits, with chronic dysbaric osteonecrosis of femoral and humeral heads. Recompression in a hyperbaric chamber is the treatment.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Respiratory regulation, high altitude & diving
questions.stem: Nitrogen narcosis in deep diving occurs because nitrogen at high partial pressure:
options: Dissolves in neural lipid membranes producing an anaesthetic effect
questions.concept: Rapture of the deep begins around 30 metres, impairing judgement. Helium-oxygen mixtures avoid it because helium is far less lipid-soluble, and are used for deep commercial diving.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Respiratory regulation, high altitude & diving
questions.stem: Cheyne-Stokes respiration is characterised by:
options: Cyclical crescendo-decrescendo breathing alternating with apnoea
questions.concept: Prolonged circulation time and increased chemoreceptor gain cause instability, seen in heart failure, at altitude and in bilateral cerebral lesions. Biot breathing is irregular and indicates medullary damage.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Respiratory regulation, high altitude & diving
questions.stem: The oxygen dissociation curve is shifted to the right by:
options: Increased carbon dioxide, hydrogen ions, temperature and 2,3-DPG
questions.concept: A rightward shift means reduced affinity, favouring tissue unloading where metabolism is high - the Bohr effect. Fetal haemoglobin and carbon monoxide shift it left, impairing release.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Respiratory regulation, high altitude & diving
questions.stem: The Haldane effect describes:
options: Increased carbon dioxide carriage by deoxygenated haemoglobin
questions.concept: Deoxygenated haemoglobin binds hydrogen ions and forms carbamino compounds more readily, so venous blood carries more carbon dioxide - the complement to the Bohr effect at the tissues.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Respiration

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: The bulk of filtered sodium is reabsorbed in:
options: The proximal convoluted tubule, about 65 percent
questions.concept: Proximal reabsorption is isosmotic and coupled to glucose, amino acids and bicarbonate. The loop reabsorbs about 25%, distal tubule 5% and collecting duct 3% under aldosterone control.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Inulin is the ideal marker for measuring glomerular filtration rate because it is:
options: Freely filtered, neither reabsorbed nor secreted nor metabolised
questions.concept: Creatinine is used clinically but is slightly secreted, overestimating GFR, and its level depends on muscle mass, which is why eGFR equations adjust for age, sex and body size.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Glucose appears in urine when the plasma level exceeds the renal threshold of approximately:
questions.concept: The transport maximum for glucose is about 375 mg/min, but splay means glucosuria begins around 180 mg/dL. SGLT2 inhibitors lower this threshold deliberately to promote glucose excretion.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Aldosterone acts principally on the:
options: Late distal tubule and collecting duct, increasing sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
questions.concept: It also promotes hydrogen ion secretion, so hyperaldosteronism causes hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis with hypertension, whereas hypoaldosteronism causes hyperkalaemic acidosis as in type 4 renal tubular acidosis.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: The countercurrent multiplier responsible for the medullary concentration gradient operates in:
options: The loop of Henle, with the vasa recta acting as countercurrent exchanger
questions.concept: Urea recycling contributes substantially to the gradient, which is why protein-malnourished patients concentrate urine poorly. Loop diuretics abolish the gradient, impairing both concentration and dilution.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: Metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap is characteristically caused by:
questions.concept: Bicarbonate loss is replaced by chloride, keeping the gap normal - hyperchloraemic acidosis. A raised gap indicates added acid, remembered as MUDPILES. Urinary anion gap distinguishes renal from gut losses.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: The main urinary buffer for excreting acid is:
options: Ammonia, forming ammonium, with phosphate as titratable acid
questions.concept: Renal ammoniagenesis from glutamine is adaptively upregulated in chronic acidosis, allowing far greater acid excretion than the fixed phosphate buffer. Its failure defines distal renal tubular acidosis.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: In respiratory acidosis, renal compensation involves:
options: Increased bicarbonate reabsorption and acid excretion, taking days to be complete
questions.concept: Acute compensation raises bicarbonate about 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg rise in PCO2, and chronic compensation about 4 mmol/L, which is why chronic retainers tolerate high PCO2 with near-normal pH.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: The micturition reflex is coordinated by:
options: The pontine micturition centre with parasympathetic S2-S4 outflow contracting the detrusor
questions.concept: Spinal cord injury above the sacral segments causes a spastic automatic bladder after spinal shock, whereas a cauda equina lesion causes a flaccid atonic bladder with overflow incontinence.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Renal tubular transport, acid-base regulation & micturition
questions.stem: The renin-angiotensin system is activated by:
options: Reduced renal perfusion pressure, reduced distal sodium delivery and sympathetic stimulation
questions.concept: Angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole preserving GFR when perfusion falls, which is why ACE inhibitors precipitate acute kidney injury in bilateral renal artery stenosis or severe hypovolaemia.
questions.reference: Ganong Review of Medical Physiology 26e, Renal Physiology
